extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, petitioners, patent owners, and counsel participating in PTAB AIA trial proceedings (IPR, PGR, CBM) and judges/panels handling those proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on institution decisions, multiple petitions, motions (including motions to amend, joinder, supplemental information), replies, and timing for PTAB AIA trial proceedings (inter partes review, post-grant review, CBM, and derivation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent owner preliminary response (waiver and effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner may elect to waive the patent owner preliminary response. No adverse inference will be taken by such an election. Moreover, a patent owner may file a statutory disclaimer of one or more challenged claims to streamline the proceedings. Where no challenged claims remain, the Board would terminate the proceeding. Where one or more challenged claims remain, the Board’s decision on institution would be based solely on the remaining claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once a trial is instituted, the Board may decline to consider arguments set forth in a preliminary response unless they are raised in the patent owner response. See In re Nuvasive (explaining that a patent owner waives an issue presented in its preliminary response if it fails to renew the issue in its response after trial is instituted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards and discretion for institution
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board institutes the trial on behalf of the Director and in deciding whether to institute will consider at a minimum whether a party has satisfied the relevant statutory institution standard (35 U.S.C. §§ 314(a), 324(a)). The Director has discretion to deny a petition under 35 U.S.C. § 314(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director’s discretion is informed by 35 U.S.C. §§ 316(b) and 326(b), which require consideration of the regulation’s effect on the economy, the integrity of the patent system, efficient administration of the Office, and the Office’s ability to timely complete proceedings. The AIA’s goals (efficiency, streamlined patent system, improved patent quality, limiting unnecessary litigation costs) inform the exercise of discretion. The Board may decline to institute based on these broader policy considerations even if threshold standards are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Plastic factors for follow-on petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-exclusive factors the Board will consider when exercising discretion on instituting inter partes review, especially for 'follow-on' petitions challenging the same patent as previously challenged:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The General Plastic factors include: (1) whether the same petitioner previously filed a petition directed to the same claims of the same patent; (2) whether at the time of filing of the first petition the petitioner knew of the prior art asserted in the second petition or should have known of it; (3) whether at the time of filing of the second petition the petitioner already received the patent owner’s preliminary response to the first petition or received the Board’s decision on whether to institute review in the first petition; (4) the length of time that elapsed between the time the petitioner learned of the prior art asserted in the second petition and the filing of the second petition; (5) whether the petitioner provides adequate explanation for the time elapsed between the filings of multiple petitions directed to the same claims of the same patent; (6) the finite resources of the Board; and (7) the requirement to issue a final determination not later than 1 year after the Director notices institution of review. General Plastic factors are not dispositive or exclusive and are part of a balanced assessment including merits. The Board also considers relationships among different petitioners and may weigh additional factors (e.g., events in other proceedings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallel/multiple petitions guidance and required disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: One petition should be sufficient in most situations; multiple petitions against the same patent at or about the same time may place substantial burden and raise fairness, timing, and efficiency concerns. Two petitions may be necessary rarely (e.g., large number of asserted claims, priority date disputes); three or more petitions by a petitioner is unlikely to be appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a petitioner files two or more petitions challenging the same patent, the petitioner should identify (1) a ranking of the petitions in the order it wishes the Board to consider the merits, and (2) a succinct explanation of differences between the petitions, why those differences are material, and why the Board should institute additional petitions. A separate paper providing this explanation is limited to the purpose and no more than 5 pages when filed with each petition. The Board encourages use of a table to identify similarities/differences. Patent owners may respond in preliminary responses (or separate 5-page papers) explaining why the Board should not exercise discretion to institute more than one petition, including by proffering stipulations that limitations are not disputed or certain references qualify as prior art. Panels may request additional papers in limited circumstances for petitions submitted before this Guide; after publication petitioners are expected to justify multiple petitions in the first instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 325(d): same or substantially the same prior art/arguments considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. § 325(d), the Director may take into account and reject a petition because the same or substantially the same prior art or arguments previously were presented to the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether to deny institution under § 325(d) is fact-dependent, balancing the petitioner’s desire to be heard against the patent owner’s interest in avoiding duplicative challenges and considering the efficient administration of the Office. The Board considers whether substantially the same art/arguments were presented previously during examination, reexamination, reissue, or an earlier petition. The Board may also consider materially changed circumstances or new evidence not previously before the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Becton Dickinson non-exclusive factors (applied to § 325(d) analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-exclusive factors the Board has considered when evaluating whether to deny institution under § 325(d):
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Becton Dickinson factors include: (1) the similarities and material differences between the asserted art and the prior art involved during examination; (2) the cumulative nature of the asserted art and the prior art evaluated during examination; (3) the extent to which the asserted art was evaluated during examination; (4) the extent of overlap between arguments made during examination and how the petitioner relies on the prior art or the patent owner distinguishes the prior art; (5) whether the petitioner has pointed out sufficiently how the Office erred in evaluating the asserted prior art; and (6) the extent to which additional evidence and facts presented in the petition warrant reconsideration. These factors are not exclusive; parties may address additional relevant factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and form of decision on whether to institute (all-or-none rule and analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: When instituting a trial, the Board will either (1) institute as to all claims challenged in the petition and on all grounds in the petition, or (2) institute on no claims and deny institution. The Board will not institute on fewer than all claims or all challenges in a petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board generally will provide analysis of the strengths and weaknesses of all challenges in the petition to guide the parties for trial. The Board retains the discretion to deny institution of the petition as a whole under 35 U.S.C. §§ 314(a) and 325(d) even when the petition includes at least one claim that otherwise meets the criteria. If a panel determines the petition meets standards for institution for fewer than all challenges, or deficiencies affect only a portion of challenges (e.g., failure to provide a § 112(f) construction), the panel will evaluate all challenges and may deny the entire petition in the interests of efficient administration and integrity of the patent system. Where no trial is instituted, the Board expects to provide a short statement as to why standards were not met (though not necessary in all cases). The Board’s determination on institution is final and nonappealable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to amend timing and confer requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent owners may file motions to amend claims subject to certain conditions (37 C.F.R. §§ 42.20, 42.121, 42.221). Although patent owners may file a first motion to amend without prior Board authorization, the patent owner is required to confer with the Board before filing the motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During a conference (call or email) the panel will provide procedural guidance to patent owner and petitioner regarding the motion. Patent owners are encouraged to contact the Board as early as possible after deciding to file to allow incorporation of guidance. A motion to amend must be filed no later than the time period for filing a patent owner response, unless a different due date is provided in a Board order. The motion-to-amend practice is under review and a pilot program offers options like requesting preliminary guidance and filing a revised motion to amend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of persuasion and evidentiary standard for substitute claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Following Aqua Products, a patent owner does not bear the burden of persuasion to demonstrate the patentability of substitute claims presented in a motion to amend. Rather, the burden of persuasion ordinarily will lie with the petitioner to show that any proposed substitute claims are unpatentable by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board may justify any finding of unpatentability by reference to evidence of record (e.g., when a petitioner ceases to participate). Ultimately, the Board determines whether substitute claims are unpatentable by a preponderance of the evidence based on the entirety of the record, including any opposition by the petitioner. If the entirety of the evidence of record is in equipoise, the Board will grant the motion to amend and the Office will issue a certificate incorporating those claims into the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents and support required in a motion to amend
rubrics_metrics.description: Any motion to amend must comply with the content requirements of 37 C.F.R. §§ 42.121(b) or 42.221(b): include a claim listing, show the changes being sought clearly, and describe how the original disclosure of the patent and any relied-upon prior application supports each claim that is added or amended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claim listing may be in an appendix. A patent owner may not enlarge the scope of the claims or add new matter (35 U.S.C. §§ 316(d)(3), 326(d)(3)). When replacing an original claim with a new claim, identify the proposed substitute claim and specify the original claim it replaces, clearly identifying all changes relative to the original claim. A patent owner should identify specifically the features added to each substitute claim and any proposed constructions for new claim terms. Although not required, patent owners may offer arguments on patentability and may support them with expert testimony (e.g., to show what a person of ordinary skill would have known and to explain significance of added features). Motions should clearly state patentably distinct features for proposed substitute claims to aid the Board in determining whether the amendment enlarges claims and if it is responsive to grounds of unpatentability. Under 37 C.F.R. § 42.11 all parties have a duty of candor, which includes the patent owner’s duty to disclose information of which the patent owner is aware that is material to the patentability of substitute claims if not already of record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on number and scope of substitute claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of substitute claims must be 'reasonable.' There is a presumption that only one substitute claim would be needed to replace each challenged claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumption may be rebutted by a demonstration of need. Motions to cancel claims will generally be permitted even late in the proceeding, as will motions to amend to correct simple and obvious typographical errors. Amendments should clearly state where the specification and drawings support all limitations in the proposed substitute claims; if the Board cannot determine support, the motion may be denied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to a motion to amend — scope and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner will be afforded an opportunity to fully respond to a patent owner's motion to amend. No authorization is needed to file an opposition to a motion to amend. Petitioners may respond to new issues and include evidence responsive to the amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes submission of new expert declarations or additional prior art directed to the proposed substitute claims. The grounds of unpatentability that can be raised in response to proposed substitute claims are not limited by 35 U.S.C. § 311(b); the Board may consider other grounds (including § 101 and § 112) as to proposed substitute claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on replies and rebuttal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner may file a reply to a patent owner response, and a patent owner may file a reply to an opposition to a motion to amend. A party may also submit rebuttal evidence in support of its reply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reply may only respond to arguments raised in the corresponding opposition (37 C.F.R. § 42.23). 'Respond' does not permit proceeding in a new direction or raising new approaches compared to the original petition or motion to amend. Replies that raise a new issue or belatedly present evidence may not be considered. Examples of new-issue indications include new evidence necessary to make out a prima facie case for patentability or unpatentability or new evidence that could have been presented earlier. The Board is not required to attempt to sort proper from improper portions of a reply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions to submit supplemental information — timing and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion to submit supplemental information must meet requirements of 37 C.F.R. §§ 42.123 or 42.223: (1) a request for authorization to file a motion to submit supplemental information must be made within one month of the date the trial is instituted; and (2) the supplemental information must be relevant to a claim for which the trial has been instituted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party seeking to submit supplemental information more than one month after institution must request authorization to file and must show why the supplemental information reasonably could not have been obtained earlier and that consideration of the information would be in the interests of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder motions — timing, conference, and discretionary factors
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may seek to join a first proceeding by filing a motion for joinder within one month of the date a trial is instituted as to the first proceeding (37 C.F.R. §§ 42.122, 42.222). A party filing a motion for joinder should arrange a conference call with the panel, petitioner, and patent owner of the first proceeding within five business days of filing the motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors the Board may consider in deciding joinder include why joinder is appropriate, whether a new ground of unpatentability is raised in the second petition, how the cost and schedule of the first proceeding will be impacted if joinder is granted, and whether granting joinder will add to complexity of briefing/discovery. The Board has discretion under 35 U.S.C. § 315(c) to join a petitioner to a proceeding and to allow joinder of new issues; existence of a time bar under § 315(b) is one of several factors the Board may consider when exercising discretion for joinder. The Board expects to exercise discretion to permit joinder only in extremely limited circumstances (e.g., certain actions by a patent owner in co-pending litigation such as late additions of newly asserted claims). The conduct of the parties and attempts to game the system may be considered. In proceedings with joinder, the Board may adjust the one-year statutory deadline for issuing a final written decision; adjustments, if possible, will not exceed an additional six months and the Board will specify any new deadline prior to expiration of the one-year period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final decision timing and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: For IPR, PGR, and CBM proceedings, the Board will enter a final written decision not more than one year from the date a trial is instituted, except that the time may be extended up to six months for good cause. The timeline may be adjusted in case of joinder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board expects that a final written decision will address the issues necessary for resolving the proceeding. In derivation proceedings, although not required by statute, the Board expects to provide a final decision not more than one year from institution, deciding whether an inventor in the earlier application derived the claimed invention and filed without authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other motions and requesting relief not identified in rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Many types of motions may be filed in a proceeding in addition to motions to amend (e.g., motions to exclude evidence, motions to seal, motions for joinder, motions to file supplemental information, motions for judgment based on supplemental information).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a party believes it has basis to request relief on a ground not identified in the rules, the party should contact the Board and arrange a conference call with the Board and opposing party to discuss the requested relief with the judge handling the proceeding. When filing the motion, the party must comply with appropriate requirements applicable to that motion type.
